chapter_summary:
Modern programming languages provide memory ordering abstractions that map to hardware fences. This chapter explores the C++ memory model and its relationship to hardware.

**C++ memory model:**

C++11 introduced a standard memory model for concurrent programming. It defines several memory ordering constraints:

1. **memory_order_seq_cst (Sequential Consistency):** The strongest ordering. All operations are ordered in a single global sequence. This is the default for `std::atomic` operations. Maps to full fences on weak hardware (MFENCE on x86, DMB on ARM).

2. **memory_order_acquire:** Ensures that all loads and stores after the acquire in program order are not reordered before the acquire. Used with lock acquisition. Maps to load fence or acquire fence.

3. **memory_order_release:** Ensures that all loads and stores before the release in program order are not reordered after the release. Used with lock release. Maps to store fence or release fence.

4. **memory_order_acq_rel:** Combines acquire and release semantics. Used with read-modify-write operations (e.g., CAS).

5. **memory_order_relaxed:** No ordering constraints. Only atomicity is guaranteed. Used for counters and flags where ordering does not matter. Maps to no fence on most hardware.

6. **memory_order_consume:** Similar to acquire but only applies to operations that are data-dependent on the loaded value. Rarely used because it is difficult to implement correctly.

**Mapping C++ memory orders to hardware:**

| C++ Order | x86 | ARM | RISC-V |
|-----------|-----|-----|--------|
| seq_cst | MFENCE (or LOCK prefix) | DMB ISH | fence rw, rw |
| acquire | (no fence needed) | DMB ISHLD | fence r, rw |
| release | (no fence needed) | DMB ISH | fence rw, w |
| acq_rel | (no fence needed) | DMB ISH | fence rw, rw |
| relaxed | (no fence) | (no fence) | (no fence) |

Note: x86's TSO is strong enough that acquire and release do not require additional fences. The compiler must only prevent compiler reordering (using compiler barriers). ARM and RISC-V require hardware fences for acquire and release.

**Performance impact:**

The performance of atomic operations depends on the memory order:
- **Relaxed:** Fastest. No fences. On x86, a relaxed atomic load is just a regular load. On ARM, it is also a regular load.
- **Acquire/Release:** Moderate. On x86, no hardware fence (but compiler barrier). On ARM, requires DMB.
- **Seq_cst:** Slowest. Requires full hardware fence on all architectures.

For example, on ARM, a `memory_order_seq_cst` operation requires a DMB (Data Memory Barrier), which can stall the pipeline for 10–20 cycles. A `memory_order_relaxed` operation has no overhead.

**Correct synchronization with fences:**

Example: Producer-consumer with a flag.
```cpp
// Producer
std::atomic<int> data(0);
std::atomic<bool> ready(false);

void producer() {
    data.store(42, std::memory_order_relaxed);
    ready.store(true, std::memory_order_release);  // Release fence
}

void consumer() {
    while (!ready.load(std::memory_order_acquire)) {}  // Acquire fence
    int value = data.load(std::memory_order_relaxed);
    // value is guaranteed to be 42
}
```

The release ensures that the store to `data` is visible before the store to `ready`. The acquire ensures that the load of `data` is not reordered before the load of `ready`. This guarantees that the consumer sees `value = 42`.

Without fences (using `memory_order_relaxed` for all operations), the compiler and hardware could reorder the stores in the producer or the loads in the consumer, and the consumer might see `value = 0`.

screens.title: Memory Ordering and Fences
screens.subtitle: How C++ memory orders map to hardware fences and why that affects correctness and performance

narration.text: In this short orientation we will set the stage for why memory ordering and fences matter when you write concurrent code. Modern CPUs and compilers reorder instructions for performance, and the C++ memory model gives you a small set of ordering tools — sequential consistency, acquire, release, acquire-release, relaxed, and consume — that constrain those reorderings. You will learn how each order maps to hardware fences on architectures like x86, ARM, and RISC-V, and when a compiler barrier is sufficient versus when you need a hardware fence. We will use concrete examples: a producer-consumer baton pass that uses acquire and release to guarantee visibility, and a performance comparison that shows relaxed is fastest and seq_cst is slowest on many platforms. Understanding these mappings helps you write correct synchronization that is also performant. By the end you will be able to choose the least restrictive memory order that preserves correctness and to explain why x86’s TSO sometimes avoids hardware fences while ARM requires explicit DMB instructions.

keyIdea.title: Core insight
keyIdea.text: Memory orders control compiler and hardware reordering. Use the weakest order that preserves correctness to minimize costly hardware fences.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: What you will be able to do after this lesson

narration.text: These four objectives focus your attention on understanding, implementing, and evaluating memory ordering. First, you will explain the different types of memory fences and how they affect instruction reordering. That means you will name seq_cst, acquire, release, acq_rel, relaxed, and consume, and describe the guarantees each provides. Second, you will implement correct synchronization using fences in C++ with std::atomic, learning to pick acquire for loads that follow a synchronization point and release for stores that publish state. Third, you will understand the C++ memory model in practice: what sequential consistency demands, how acquire-release composes, and when relaxed is acceptable. Finally, you will analyze performance implications of orders, comparing relaxed, acquire/release, and seq_cst on architectures that require hardware fences versus those that rely on stronger default ordering. Each objective includes a small mnemonic or milestone to verify competency so you can practice and measure correctness and performance.

screens.title: C++ memory orders — vocabulary and guarantees
screens.subtitle: Define seq_cst, acquire, release, acq_rel, relaxed, and consume

narration.text: We begin by defining each memory order and the guarantee it provides. Sequential consistency, or seq_cst, is the strongest: it gives the illusion of a single global order of all atomic operations. Acquire prevents later memory accesses from moving before the acquire; use it on loads that observe a published state. Release prevents earlier operations from moving after the release; use it on stores that publish state. Acquire-release composes both directions and is suitable for read-modify-write operations. Relaxed provides only atomicity and no ordering; it is useful for counters where no ordering is required. Consume is like acquire but constrained to data-dependent uses; it is rarely used because of portability and implementation difficulties. A concrete example helps: when a producer stores data and then sets a ready flag with release, and a consumer waits on ready with an acquire load, acquire-release guarantees the consumer will see the prior data stores. A common misconception is that relaxed is 'safe enough' for visibility — relaxed only guarantees atomic updates, not visibility ordering. Takeaway: learn the guarantee first, then apply the weakest ordering that preserves correctness.

keyIdea.title: Definitions matter
keyIdea.text: Each memory order gives specific reordering constraints; pick the weakest that preserves correctness to avoid unnecessary fences.

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 11.6 › C++ memory orders
Order definitions
  • seq_cst — single global sequence for atomics.
  • acquire — prevents later memory accesses from moving before the load.
  • release — prevents earlier accesses from moving after the store.
  • acq_rel — combined acquire and release for read-modify-write.
  • relaxed — atomicity only, no ordering guarantees.
  • consume — acquire-like for data-dependent uses; rarely used.
Key Takeaway

Understand the specific reordering each order prohibits, then choose the weakest order that still guarantees correctness.

Concrete example
// Producer
std::atomic data(0);
std::atomic ready(false);

void producer() {
  data.store(42, std::memory_order_relaxed);
  ready.store(true, std::memory_order_release);
}

// Consumer
void consumer() {
  while (!ready.load(std::memory_order_acquire)) {}
  int value = data.load(std::memory_order_relaxed);
  // value == 42 guaranteed
}
This pattern shows release on the publisher and acquire on the observer to order the data store with the ready flag.
Common mistake

Using relaxed for both data and flag allows reorderings; the consumer might read stale data. Always use release/acquire pair where visibility ordering matters.

screens.title: Mapping memory orders to hardware
screens.subtitle: How seq_cst, acquire, release and relaxed map to fences on x86, ARM, and RISC-V

narration.text: Mapping C++ memory orders to hardware is essential to understand the real cost of synchronization. The chapter provides a concise table: seq_cst maps to a full fence such as MFENCE on x86, DMB ISH on ARM, and fence rw, rw on RISC-V. Acquire and release semantics often map to lighter fences on weak architectures: ARM uses DMB ISHLD for acquire and DMB ISH for release; RISC-V emits targeted fence forms. x86’s Total Store Order gives it stronger default guarantees, so acquire and release typically do not emit hardware fences on x86; the compiler must still prevent compiler reordering. Relaxed maps to no fence on most hardware. A concrete example of this mapping: a load with acquire on ARM will need a DMB to avoid later loads being reordered before it; on x86, the hardware already prevents that reorder. A common misconception is assuming the same cost across processors — seq_cst cost can vary but often requires a heavyweight fence on all architectures. Takeaway: knowing the hardware mapping lets you predict latency and choose orders that minimize pipeline stalls while keeping correctness.

keyIdea.title: Hardware mapping
keyIdea.text: x86 TSO reduces fence needs for acquire/release; ARM and RISC-V require explicit fences for ordering.

Concrete implication

On ARM, an acquire load must be followed by a DMB to prevent later reads from moving before it. On x86, the hardware already provides that ordering, so compilers only emit compiler barriers. This difference is why acquire/release costs more on ARM than on x86 in many benchmarks.

Pro tip

When portability matters, assume weaker hardware: add acquire/release fences where needed and measure performance on target CPUs.

screens.title: Acquire-release synchronization pattern
screens.subtitle: How release and acquire create a happens-before relationship

narration.text: Acquire-release is a practical synchronization idiom that creates a happens-before relationship between two threads. The producer performs all necessary stores to shared data, then performs a store with release semantics to publish a flag. The consumer spins or waits until a load with acquire returns true, and once the acquire returns it sees all prior stores made visible by the producer. Concretely, imagine the producer writes the payload value into a data variable with relaxed ordering, then sets ready with release. The consumer performs an acquire load on ready and then reads the data value with relaxed. Acquire prevents the consumer's load of data from being reordered before the load that observed ready. A common misconception is that release alone guarantees the consumer sees data without acquire; both sides participate. Another pitfall is relying on compiler barriers only on weak hardware — on ARM you need the hardware DMB to enforce ordering. Takeaway: acquire-release composes to guarantee the correct baton pass when both sides use the correct orders. Acquire-release synchronization pattern means a release store plus an acquire load forms a synchronization edge that ensures visibility of prior writes.. In practical terms, how release and acquire create a happens-before relationship. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Acquire-release rule
keyIdea.text: A release store plus an acquire load forms a synchronization edge that ensures visibility of prior writes.

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 11.6 › Acquire-release pattern
Step 1 — Producer
Write payload (relaxed or normal store). Then publish by storing true to ready with memory_order_release so prior stores cannot move past the release.
Step 2 — Consumer
Wait on ready using load with memory_order_acquire. Once the acquire succeeds, subsequent loads will see the published payload.
Key Takeaway

Both sides must use the matching orders: release to publish, acquire to consume. The pair creates a happens-before edge.

Concrete scenario
Producer stores sequence: write buffer, write metadata, release store to ready. Consumer loops until acquire load on ready is true, then reads buffer and metadata safely.
Common mistake
If the producer uses relaxed for the publish store, or the consumer uses relaxed for the waiter, there is no ordering guarantee and stale reads can occur.
Check: can you point to the store that must be release, and the load that must be acquire in your own code?

screens.title: Producer-consumer example (acquire/release)
screens.subtitle: Walkthrough of the canonical publish-consume pattern in C++

narration.text: Let's walk through the producer-consumer example step by step. The code uses two std::atomic variables: data and ready. The producer stores the payload into data with relaxed ordering. That store can be non-fenced because it is not the publishing action. Immediately after, the producer sets ready to true with memory_order_release — this is the publish action that prevents earlier stores from being reordered after the flag. The consumer spins on ready using load with memory_order_acquire; once it observes true, the acquire prevents subsequent loads (the read of data) from moving before the load that observed ready. The result is the consumer reads the value stored by the producer. A common misconception is that marking both as relaxed will still work because atomics are atomic; this is false because relaxed does not order the operations. Another misconception is that seq_cst is always needed; seq_cst is stronger but often unnecessary and more expensive. Takeaway: release on publisher and acquire on consumer is correct and performant on most hardware when used intentionally. Producer-consumer example (acquire/release) means use relaxed for payload stores and release for the flag store; consumer uses acquire for the flag to ensure visibility.. In practical terms, walkthrough of the canonical publish-consume pattern in c++. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Producer-consumer
keyIdea.text: Use relaxed for payload stores and release for the flag store; consumer uses acquire for the flag to ensure visibility.

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 11.6 › Producer-consumer example
Canonical code
// Producer
std::atomic data(0);
std::atomic ready(false);

void producer() {
  data.store(42, std::memory_order_relaxed);
  ready.store(true, std::memory_order_release);
}

// Consumer
void consumer() {
  while (!ready.load(std::memory_order_acquire)) {}
  int value = data.load(std::memory_order_relaxed);
  // value is guaranteed to be 42
}
Explanation
  • data.store is relaxed because ordering is provided by the flag.
  • ready.store uses release to publish prior writes.
  • ready.load uses acquire so subsequent reads see published data.
Check your understanding
Why is acquire required on the consumer for correctness? What could go wrong if it were relaxed?

screens.title: Performance implications of memory orders
screens.subtitle: Why relaxed < acquire/release < seq_cst in typical cost

narration.text: Memory ordering choices have measurable performance effects. Relaxed operations are fastest because they emit no fences and let the hardware run freely. Acquire and release add ordering constraints; on x86 these often require only compiler barriers because TSO already offers the necessary guarantees, so the hardware cost is low. On ARM and RISC-V, acquire and release may require a DMB or fence instruction, which stalls memory ordering and can cost tens of cycles. Seq_cst typically emits full fences and is the heaviest. A concrete experiment from the hands-on activity is to implement three spinlock variants: seq_cst everywhere, acquire on lock and release on unlock, and relaxed everywhere. Measuring 1 million lock/unlock iterations across four threads will show relaxed as fastest but incorrect, seq_cst as correct but slowest, and acquire/release as correct and often faster than seq_cst. A common misconception is that seq_cst only affects single instructions — it affects global ordering and can force heavy fences. Takeaway: measure on your target C P U and prefer the weakest ordering that maintains correctness. Performance implications of memory orders means relaxed is cheapest; acquire/release has moderate cost depending on hardware; seq_cst often requires full fences and is most expensive.. In practical terms, why relaxed < acquire/release < seq_cst in typical cost. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Performance order
keyIdea.text: Relaxed is cheapest; acquire/release has moderate cost depending on hardware; seq_cst often requires full fences and is most expensive.

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 11.6 › Performance implications
Relative cost (typical)
Relaxed < Acquire/Release < Seq_cst. On ARM, acquire/release often requires DMB, increasing latency. On x86, acquire/release often avoids hardware fences due to TSO.
Experiment
Implement three spinlock variants and measure 1,000,000 acquisitions with 4 threads. Compare timings to observe the cost of fences.
Practical recommendation
Prefer acquire/release for synchronization patterns. Use seq_cst only when you need global ordering. Use relaxed only when you can prove ordering is irrelevant.
Pro tip

Measure on the target architecture because fence costs vary significantly between x86 and ARM.

screens.title: Compiler barriers vs hardware fences
screens.subtitle: Why both are necessary and how they differ

narration.text: Compiler barriers and hardware fences serve related but distinct roles. A compiler barrier prevents the compiler from reordering instructions during optimization, so source-level instruction order is preserved across the barrier. However, it emits no machine instruction that affects the C P U's memory ordering. A hardware fence, such as MFENCE on x86 or DMB on ARM, prevents the processor and memory system from reordering operations at runtime. Both are needed because reordering can occur both at compile time and at execution time. A concrete example: on x86 a memory_order_acquire may be implemented as a compiler barrier only because x86 TSO already prevents the processor from performing the dangerous reorder, while on ARM the same memory_order_acquire requires a DMB to enforce ordering in hardware. A common misconception is that a compiler fence is sufficient on all hardware; on weakly ordered architectures it is not. Takeaway: ensure your atomic implementation provides both a compiler barrier and the required hardware fence for the target architecture to get correct synchronization. Compiler barriers vs hardware fences means compiler barriers stop compile-time reorders; hardware fences stop runtime reorders. both are required on weakly ordered hardware.. In practical terms, why both are necessary and how they differ. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Two-layer protection
keyIdea.text: Compiler barriers stop compile-time reorders; hardware fences stop runtime reorders. Both are required on weakly ordered hardware.

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 11.6 › Compiler vs Hardware
Compiler barrier
Stops the optimizer from reordering memory operations across the barrier. It does not emit a CPU instruction that affects memory ordering at runtime.
Hardware fence
Emits a CPU instruction that prevents the processor or memory system from reordering operations, for example MFENCE or DMB.
Example
On x86, acquire often needs only a compiler barrier because TSO forbids the hazardous reorders. On ARM, acquire requires a DMB fence so that the hardware does not reorder subsequent loads before the acquire.
Common mistake
Relying on compiler barriers alone on weak architectures leads to incorrect behavior because the processor can still reorder at runtime.

screens.title: x86 TSO versus ARM weak ordering
screens.subtitle: How architectural guarantees change the fence requirements

narration.text: Different C P U memory models change what fences are required. x86 implements Total Store Order, which guarantees that stores appear in program order to other processors and that loads are not reordered before earlier stores from the same thread. As a result, acquire and release semantics typically do not need additional hardware fences on x86. ARM and RISC-V implement weaker models where loads and stores can be reordered more freely, so acquire and release usually require DMB or fence instructions. A practical consequence: the same C++ program may instrument different instructions on different architectures; on x86 the compiler may only insert compiler barriers for acquire, while on ARM it must also emit a DMB. A common misconception is that hardware behaves uniformly; this is not true. Takeaway: when writing portable concurrent code, assume weak ordering at the hardware level and rely on the C++ memory model to emit the correct fences for your target architectures. x86 TSO versus ARM weak ordering means x86 tso reduces fence needs; arm and risc-v need explicit fences to enforce acquire/release semantics.. In practical terms, how architectural guarantees change the fence requirements. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Architectural difference
keyIdea.text: x86 TSO reduces fence needs; ARM and RISC-V need explicit fences to enforce acquire/release semantics.

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 11.6 › x86 vs ARM
x86 TSO
Stronger default ordering reduces need for hardware fences for acquire/release. Compilers still insert compiler barriers when required.
ARM / RISC-V
Weaker memory models allow more reorderings, so acquire and release typically map to DMB or fence instructions to enforce ordering.
Practical tip
When writing portable code, program to the C++ memory model and test on your target architecture. Assume weak ordering if unsure.

screens.title: Spinlock experiment and measurement plan
screens.subtitle: Implement three spinlock versions and compare timings

narration.text: The hands-on activity asks you to implement three spinlock variants and measure their performance. Version one uses memory_order_seq_cst for all operations; it is simple but often slow because it may require full fences. Version two uses memory_order_acquire for the lock acquisition and memory_order_release for unlock. This version is correct and frequently faster because it uses the weaker ordering needed for synchronization. Version three uses memory_order_relaxed for all operations; it is usually incorrect but included to measure the cost and to demonstrate visibility failures. Your measurement plan: run four threads contending for the lock, perform one million acquire/release pairs per thread, and record elapsed time. Observe the relative timings and check correctness by ensuring released critical sections protect shared state. A common error is forgetting to use release on unlock — that breaks the guarantee. Takeaway: implementing and measuring these three variants makes the trade-offs concrete and helps you pick an appropriate ordering for real systems. Version 1
Use memory_order_seq_cst for lock and unlock. Correct but potentially slow due to full fences.

screens.title: Common synchronization mistakes
screens.subtitle: Relaxed misuse, partial fences, and incorrect assumptions about hardware

narration.text: Developers commonly make a few recurring mistakes with memory ordering. The first is using memory_order_relaxed for convenience when ordering matters; relaxed only guarantees atomicity and does not prevent reorderings, so visibility bugs appear. The second is applying a fence on only one side of a synchronization and assuming the other side will magically get the ordering; both sides must use compatible orders for the happens-before relationship. Third, assuming x86 and ARM behave the same leads to portability bugs — x86 TSO can hide bugs that break on ARM. Fourth, overusing seq_cst because it seems safer; this can create unnecessary performance bottlenecks. A concrete scenario: publishing a pointer with relaxed store while the writer updates the pointee before the store — the reader may see the pointer but not the initialized contents. The fix is release on the publisher and acquire on the consumer. Takeaway: reason about the required ordering for each synchronization edge and enforce it on both sides. Common synchronization mistakes means do not rely on relaxed when ordering is required; apply matching acquire/release on both sides and test on weakly ordered hardware.. In practical terms, relaxed misuse, partial fences, and incorrect assumptions about hardware. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Avoid these errors
keyIdea.text: Do not rely on relaxed when ordering is required; apply matching acquire/release on both sides and test on weakly ordered hardware.

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 11.6 › Common mistakes
Relaxed misuse
Relaxed does not order memory. Use it only when you can prove ordering is irrelevant, such as simple counters that do not coordinate other memory.
Partial fences
Fencing only the publisher or only the consumer is insufficient; both sides must participate to form a happens-before edge.
Portability assumption
Code that relies on x86 TSO behavior without explicit memory orders may break on ARM. Always program to the C++ model for portability.
Overusing seq_cst
seq_cst is easiest to reason about but can be a performance anti-pattern. Use it only when global ordering is required.
Quick fix
When in doubt, use acquire on loads that wait and release on the corresponding store that publishes data. Then test on target hardware.

screens.title: Practical rules for choosing memory orders
screens.subtitle: A short checklist to make safe, efficient choices

narration.text: Here are practical rules you can apply when choosing memory orders. Rule one: think about the synchronization edge and the happens-before relationship you need. If a store must be visible before another thread proceeds, use release on the store and acquire on the waiting load. Rule two: prefer relaxed only for independent counters or metrics that do not affect other memory. Rule three: reserve seq_cst for cases that require a single global ordering across many operations; avoid it for fine-grained locks. narration.text: These practical takeaways will guide your work. First, the producer-consumer pattern is the canonical example of acquire-release correctness: data is stored, then a release publishes a flag; the consumer uses acquire to read the flag and then sees the data. Second, compiler barriers prevent compile-time reorders, but hardware fences prevent runtime reorders; both are relevant on weakly ordered architectures.
